intro: Joan Benson plays Bach’s late F♯ minor Fantasia on the clavichord, an instrument whose quiet voice can still snap from a whisper to an outburst. Long runs spill beyond the bar lines; little chords stop them short.

sections.label: A · Chords break into a run
sections.mNote: Two measured bars give way to free passagework

sections.label: B · Runs and quick replies
sections.mNote: Short figures gather into longer streams of notes

sections.label: C · Notes separated by rests
sections.mNote: The clavichord’s short phrases leave gaps between them

sections.label: D · Chords interrupt the runs
sections.mNote: Quick figures meet sharply accented chords

sections.label: E · Quiet phrases and pauses
sections.mNote: Small gestures leave room for the strings to fade

sections.label: F · Running notes return
sections.mNote: Flourishes and chordal replies share the keyboard

sections.label: Coda · Towards the final Largo
sections.mNote: The closing melody settles over repeated F♯s

cues.title: Two bars, then freedom
cues.text: Adagio. Small pairs of chords sound above a steady bass, separated by rests. After two measured bars, the music breaks loose: a run rises through the keyboard, and the bar lines disappear. Sudden piano and forte markings interrupt one another within a single phrase.
cues.evidence: Score, Liam Hynes transcription, p. 1, bars 1–3. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/5/5b/IMSLP283144-PMLP459537-C.P.E._Bach_F-sharp_minor_Phantasy.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A pianist starts again
cues.text: Benson arrives at Fritz Neumeyer’s clavichord lessons as an accomplished pianist. He refuses to let her play pieces at first. For months she works only on making a tone. Recalling those lessons in 1999, she says, “I had to become a beginner again”.
cues.evidence: Joan Benson interviewed by Richard Troeger, Boston Clavichord Society Newsletter 7, autumn 1999; recollection of lessons in Freiburg before 1960. https://joanbenson.com/articles-about-joan-benson/an-interview-with-clavichordist-joan-benson/

cues.title: Bach’s rule for moving people
cues.text: “A musician cannot move others unless he too is moved.” Bach writes this in his 1753 keyboard treatise. He singles out improvisations and fantasias as places where the player can most directly command an audience’s feelings.
cues.evidence: C. P. E. Bach, Versuch über die wahre Art das Clavier zu spielen, part I (1753), chapter 3, §13; William J. Mitchell translation (1948), p. 152, quoted in The Essential C. P. E. Bach, introduction, p. xix. https://www.cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/Essential-CPEB-Intro.pdf

cues.title: Nearly eleven in Hamburg
cues.text: After dinner in Hamburg in 1772, Bach sits at his clavichord for Charles Burney. He plays until nearly eleven. Burney watches his fixed eyes, fallen lower lip and gathering sweat; the little instrument has its player completely absorbed.
cues.evidence: Charles Burney’s account of his 1772 visit, published in The Present State of Music in Germany, the Netherlands, and United Provinces (1775), vol. 2, p. 269; quoted in The Essential C. P. E. Bach, p. xiv. https://www.cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/Essential-CPEB-Intro.pdf

cues.title: Benson tries to make a cut
cues.text: Preparing this fantasia for a 1961 radio appearance, Benson considers shortening it. She finds she cannot: each section leads into the next. In her 1999 interview with Richard Troeger, she recalls finding the connection in the bass line and allowing the piece to change with every performance.
cues.evidence: Benson’s recollection of preparing Wq 67 for KQED in 1961, in Richard Troeger’s 1999 interview. https://joanbenson.com/articles-about-joan-benson/an-interview-with-clavichordist-joan-benson/

cues.title: A recording among the stars
cues.text: Benson’s first recording sessions in 1962 need three locations. Cleaners interrupt one; a radio station intrudes on another. Finally, a house in Marin County gives her quiet. Between takes she goes outside to look at the stars or pet the dog.
cues.evidence: Benson recounts the 1962 Repertoire Records sessions to Richard Troeger in 1999. This is the history of her first record; the Commons transfer does not document its own session date. https://joanbenson.com/articles-about-joan-benson/an-interview-with-clavichordist-joan-benson/

cues.title: Largo over repeated F♯s
cues.text: The last Largo brings back bar lines and a twelve-eight metre. Repeated low F♯s hold the music in place while the right hand makes its final turns. The last phrase is marked pianissimo; rests follow the closing chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Frederick the Great’s accompanist wrote keyboard music that breaks off mid-sentence and makes a single note tremble.
facts: His father, Johann Sebastian Bach; studied law in Leipzig and Frankfurt an der Oder
Frederick II’s harpsichordist, 1740–67 · Hamburg music director, 1768–88
Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments, 1753 and 1762
Wq: Alfred Wotquenne · H: E. Eugene Helm

quote.text: A musician can move others only if he is moved himself.
quote.source: Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments, Part I, chapter 3, §13 (1753); our translation

composer.background:
On 12 October 1772, Charles Burney went to dinner with Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach in Hamburg. Bach’s wife, his lawyer son, his daughter and three or four friends were there; upstairs was a music room hung with pictures, drawings and prints of more than a hundred and fifty musicians. Before dinner Bach had played his Silbermann clavichord; afterwards Burney talked him back to the keyboard, and he played almost until eleven. His eyes became fixed, his lower lip dropped, and Burney watched a sociable host disappear into his own music. On a long note, Burney wrote, Bach could draw from the clavichord “a cry of sorrow and complaint”.

Emanuel was born in Weimar on 8 March 1714, the second surviving son of Johann Sebastian Bach and Maria Barbara. Telemann was his godfather. The household moved to Cöthen in 1717 and Leipzig in 1723, when Sebastian became Thomaskantor. Visiting musicians came to play for his father; the boy heard them at home. “In composition and keyboard playing I never had any teacher other than my father,” he wrote in the autobiography published in 1773.
